meta.prompt: You are a worldclass math professor with expertise in breaking down math problem || Problem: In triangle $PQR$, side $PQ = 30$, side $QR = 40$, and the included angle at $Q$ measures $90°$. Find the l

steps.description: We have triangle $PQR$ with a **right angle at $Q$**, so $PR$ is the **hypotenuse** — the side directly across from the right angle. The two legs are $PQ = 30$ and $QR = 40$. This is a classic right-triangle problem: use the **Pythagorean theorem** to find the missing side, then use **trigonometry** to find the missing angle.
steps.title: Understand the Setup

steps.description:
For any right triangle, the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the two legs squared:
$$PR^2 = PQ^2 + QR^2 = 30^2 + 40^2 = 900 + 1600 = 2500$$

Recognizing $2500 = 50^2$ immediately gives us:
$$PR = 50$$

This is the famous **3-4-5 Pythagorean triple**, scaled by a factor of $10$.
steps.title: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem

steps.description:
Angle $P$ is at vertex $P$. Looking from $P$, the side **opposite** is $QR = 40$ and the side **adjacent** is $PQ = 30$. Tangent is opposite over adjacent:
$$\tan(P) = \frac{QR}{PQ} = \frac{40}{30} = \frac{4}{3}$$

Applying the inverse tangent:
$$P = \arctan\!\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx 53.13° \approx \mathbf{53°}$$
steps.title: Find Angle P with Tangent

meta.prompt: You are a worldclass math professor with expertise in breaking down math problem || Problem: In circle $O$, the radius is $r = 13$. Chord $AB$ is drawn such that it is perpendicular to radius $OC$ at

steps.description:
We have a circle with center $O$ and radius $r = 13$. A chord $AB$ is drawn, and a radius $OC$ drops **perpendicularly** onto $AB$ at point $M$, where $OM = 5$.

The key geometric fact: **a radius drawn perpendicular to a chord always bisects that chord**. This means $M$ is the exact midpoint of $AB$, so $AM = MB$.

This creates a right triangle $OMA$, where:
- $OA$ = radius = $13$ (hypotenuse)
- $OM$ = perpendicular distance from center to chord = $5$ (one leg)
- $AM$ = half the chord length = **unknown** (other leg)

The Pythagorean theorem will unlock the answer directly.
steps.title: Understand the Setup

steps.description:
In right triangle $OMA$, the hypotenuse is the radius $OA = 13$:
$$OA^2 = OM^2 + AM^2$$
$$13^2 = 5^2 + AM^2$$
$$169 = 25 + AM^2$$
$$AM^2 = 144$$
$$AM = 12$$

So the **half-chord** length is $12$.
steps.title: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem

steps.description:
Since $M$ bisects $AB$, both halves are equal: $AM = MB = 12$.
$$AB = AM + MB = 12 + 12 = 24$$
steps.title: Find Full Chord Length

meta.prompt: You are a worldclass math professor with expertise in breaking down math problem || Problem: A regular hexagon has a side length of $12$ cm. (a) Find the perimeter of the hexagon. (b) Find the measure

response.final_answer:
**(a)** Perimeter $= 72$ cm

**(b)** Each interior angle $= 120°$

**(c)** Area of one triangle $= 36\sqrt{3}$ cm²

Total area of hexagon $= 216\sqrt{3}$ cm²

steps.description:
A **regular hexagon** has all 6 sides equal and all 6 angles equal. With side length $s = 12$ cm, we need to find:
- **(a)** The perimeter — total distance around the outside
- **(b)** Each interior angle — using the polygon angle formula
- **(c)** The total area — by splitting the hexagon into 6 equilateral triangles from the center

The key insight for part (c): a regular hexagon is made of exactly **6 congruent equilateral triangles**, each with the same side length as the hexagon. This is the elegant shortcut that makes area easy.
steps.title: Understand the Problem

steps.description:
A regular hexagon has **6 equal sides**, so the perimeter is simply:
$$P = 6 \times s = 6 \times 12 = 72 \text{ cm}$$
steps.title: Find the Perimeter

steps.description:
For any **regular polygon** with $n$ sides, the sum of all interior angles is $(n-2) \times 180°$. Dividing by $n$ gives each individual angle.

With $n = 6$:
$$\text{Each interior angle} = \frac{(6-2) \times 180°}{6} = \frac{4 \times 180°}{6} = \frac{720°}{6} = 120°$$
steps.title: Find Each Interior Angle

steps.description:
Drawing lines from the center to each of the 6 vertices splits the hexagon into **6 identical triangles**. Each triangle has:
- Two sides that are radii of the hexagon
- One side that is a side of the hexagon ($12$ cm)

Since the hexagon is regular, by symmetry each of the 6 central angles equals $\frac{360°}{6} = 60°$. Two sides of each triangle are equal (both radii), and the angle between them is $60°$ — this forces all three angles to be $60°$, making every triangle **equilateral** with side length $12$ cm.
steps.title: Identify the 6 Equilateral Triangles

steps.description:
The area of an equilateral triangle with side $a$ is derived by dropping a height $h$ from the apex to the base, splitting it into two 30-60-90 triangles:
$$h = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$$

So the area is:
$$A_{\triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times a \times h = \frac{1}{2} \times a \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2$$

Substituting $a = 12$:
$$A_{\triangle} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 12^2 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 144 = 36\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2$$
steps.title: Area of One Equilateral Triangle

steps.description:
Since the hexagon is made of **6 congruent equilateral triangles**:
$$A_{\text{hexagon}} = 6 \times A_{\triangle} = 6 \times 36\sqrt{3} = 216\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2$$
steps.title: Total Area of the Hexagon
